figures.shows: Left: a three-qubit VQPM circuit with Ry(theta2), Ry(theta1), Ry(theta0) gates on qubits q2, q1, q0, a controlled unitary U driven by a control qubit q3 between two Hadamard gates, and a measurement M with a 'lock?' box on each of q2, q1, q0. Right: a workflow loop Initial State, Apply V = I + U, Measure, then Lock Qubits when the success probability of any qubit is above 50 percent, then Repeat.
figures.confirmed_by: The overall circuit depicted for three qubits and summary of the VQPM workflow with locking mechanism

figures.shows: Panel (a): function value (y, 0 to about 0.7) against k (x, 1 to 10) for x^k and cos^2k(1 - x/2) at x = 0.30 and x = 0.70; all four series fall as k grows, and the cosine-power series lie below the matching x^k series. Panel (b): cos(x) (y, 0 to 1) for x from -pi/2 to pi/2, a single arch with peak 1 at x = 0 and 0 at both ends.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2: Cosine function and its power.

figures.shows: Left: energy landscape, QUBO value (y, about -20 to about 40) against state index (x, 0 to about 32000, so n = 15); a red 'Target' marker sits near index 25000 at the bottom of the landscape, near -18. Right: convergence progress, success probability (y, 0 to about 0.065) against iteration (x, 0 to 2000); the Algorithm curve rises to about 0.026 near iteration 500 and then falls back to about 0, below the 'Polynomial line (1/n)' at about 0.067.
figures.confirmed_by: Incorrect convergence may be caused by bias in the probabilities of the qubits from the early measurement results.

figures.shows: VQPM without locking. (a) n = 15, 100 trials: bar chart of different bits per trial (0 to about 7, dashed mean line labelled 1.49) and convergence curves of success probability (y, 0 to 0.4) against iteration (x, 0 to 500); the mean (black) rises to about 0.065, near the 1/n line, and individual trials reach up to about 0.38. (b) n = 1 to 18, 500 iterations max: mean different bits rises from 0 to about 1.55; mean final success probability falls from about 0.6 at n = 1 to about 0.03 at n = 18, above the 1/2^n line and, from about n = 8 onward, below the 1/n line.
figures.confirmed_by: As can be seen from the lower right side of the figure, the mean success probability approaches the exponential line, which indicates that the convergence is still bounded by the eigengap.

figures.shows: Two n = 15 QUBO trials with locking. (a) Energy landscape (QUBO value, about -33 to about 15, over state index 0 to about 32000) with target and found markers at the same low point near index 12000; the convergence curve (success probability against iteration, 0 to 9) rises to about 0.13 at iteration 9, above the 1/n line at about 0.067 from iteration 7. (b) Another landscape (value about -22 to about 20) with target near index 11000; the curve rises to about 0.008 by iteration 6 to 8 and falls to 0 at iteration 9.

figures.shows: VQPM with fixed pdiff = 0.01, precision 3. (a) n = 15, 100 trials: different bits per trial (dashed mean line, labelled 1.16) and convergence curves over 30 iterations; the mean (black) reaches about 0.15, many single trials step up to plateaus near 0.25 or 0.5, and one reaches 1.0. (b) n = 1 to 18, 30 iterations max: mean different bits rises from 0 to about 1.75; mean final success probability is about 0.58 at n = 1, peaks near 0.78 at n = 2, and falls to about 0.19 at n = 18, above both the 1/2^n and 1/n lines.

figures.shows: VQPM with a dynamic pdiff from Hoeffding's inequality. (a) n = 15, 100 trials: different bits per trial (mean line labelled 1.31) and convergence curves over 30 iterations; the mean reaches about 0.14. (b) n = 1 to 18: mean different bits rises from 0 to about 1.72; mean final success probability goes from about 0.58 at n = 1 to a peak of about 0.68 at n = 2, and falls to about 0.18 at n = 18.

figures.shows: n = 8, 100 random QUBO trials, VQPM against QAOA with p = 8. Left: final target-state probability (y, 0 to 1) per trial; VQPM points cluster at about 0.5 (some at 0 or 1.0), QAOA points range from about 0.2 to 1.0; mean lines labelled VQPM = 0.43 and QAOA = 0.55. Right: bar chart of different bits per trial (0 to about 5); mean lines labelled VQPM = 0.43 and QAOA = 0.33.
figures.confirmed_by: The empirical results indicate that under these specific parameters, QAOA outperforms VQPM on both evaluative metrics

figures.shows: Scaling for n = 4 to 16 in steps of 2, 10 trials per step, VQPM and QAOA with p = 2, 4, 6, 8. Left: average different bits (y, 0 to about 2.2); all series spike at n = 10 (VQPM about 1.1, QAOA p = 2 about 2.2, p = 4 about 1.4, p = 6 about 1.1, p = 8 about 0.6); VQPM is about 0.2 at n = 12 and n = 14. Right: average target-state probability (y, 0 to about 0.75); QAOA p = 8 falls from about 0.70 at n = 4 to about 0.18 at n = 16, p = 2 from about 0.37 to about 0.02; VQPM stays between about 0.2 and about 0.46, peaking at n = 12.
figures.confirmed_by: As illustrated in Fig. 10, the advantages of deep-circuit QAOA configurations at small qubit numbers quickly diminish as the dimension of the underlying Hilbert space expands exponentially.

figures.shows: Twelve panels, one per qubit (qubits 1 to 12), of P(1) against iteration (x, 0 to about 82) for an 'Original' (noiseless) series and a 'Quantum' (noisy) series. In the noisy series, qubits 1 to 7 and 10 jump to 0 or 1.0 (qubits 1 and 6 go to 0; qubits 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 10 go to 1.0) at iterations from about 8 to about 60; qubits 8, 9, 11 and 12 stay between about 0.47 and about 0.52 to the end, while the noiseless series locks qubits 8, 9 and 11 at about iteration 82, 60 and 46. Qubit 12 is unlocked in both: noiseless P(1) climbs to about 0.54, noisy P(1) peaks at about 0.516 and falls to about 0.47.
figures.confirmed_by: The high pdiff setting delays locking but cannot overcome measurement noise at 100,000 shots per qubit.

papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of the variational quantum power method (VQPM) with qubit locking on random QUBO problems, compared against QAOA and tested under simulated noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that in VQPM the power-iteration algorithm is converted into a variational circuit by adding rotational-Y gates to the qubits that represent eigenstates.
quotes: the algorithm is converted into a variational circuit by adding rotational-Y gates to the qubits representing eigenstates.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the VQPM circuit construction in Section 2.1.

assertions.value: The authors define qubit locking: if the probability difference between 0 and 1 for a qubit is larger than the parameter pdiff, the qubit is locked to 0 or 1 depending on the outcome, for the rest of the iterations.
quotes: That means if the probability difference between 0 and 1 for any qubit is larger than an optimization parameter pdiff , then the values of these qubits are locked to {0, 1} depending on the outcome.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the locking rule in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that after k iterations the overlap with the target eigenstate is proportional to the kth power of the ratio R of cosines of half the eigenphases, and that the success probability scales with R raised to the power 2k.
quotes: After k iterations, the overlap of the collapsed state with the target eigenstate |d⟩ becomes proportional to the
However, the success probability scales with R2k.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper gives a derivation sketch with no theorem statement or conditions in a quotable form.

assertions.value: The authors assume that all eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian are non-negative and in the range 0 to pi over 2, so that the magnitude 2 times the absolute cosine of lambda over 2 decreases as lambda increases.
quotes: Assuming that all eigenvalues of H are non-negative and in the range [0, π/2], this magnitude decreases as λj increases
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this assumption for its analysis in Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that on quantum computers the dominant eigenvector can be obtained even when the Hamiltonian has degenerate minimum energies, if it is in the superposition with a probability on the order of 1/n.

figures.shows: a mind-map of the book with centre 'ML in quantum sciences' and four coloured branches, each tagged with section or chapter numbers. Learning from data: unsupervised (sec. 3.2, 3.4, 7.2), supervised (sec. 3.3, 4.5, 7.3) and reinforcement learning (ch. 6). Principles of ML: bias-variance trade-off (sec. 2.2), interpretability (sec. 3.5), automatic differentiation (sec. 2.5, 7.1) and statistical physics for ML (sec. 8.1). Task: classification (ch. 3, sec. 4.2.2), regression (ch. 4, sec. 7.3.2), sampling and density estimation (sec. 7.2). Architecture: classical (CNN sec. 2.4.4 and 3.3, 3.5.2; NF sec. 7.2.1; RNN sec. 2.4.6 and 5.2.2; kernel methods ch. 4; AE sec. 2.4.5 and 3.4.1) and quantum (sec. 8.2). Application: phase classification (ch. 3), representation of quantum states (ch. 5), quantum computing (sec. 6.6.4 to 6.6.5), quantum chemistry (sec. 4.5) and quantum experiments (optimization and speed-up sec. 6.6.3 and 7.3.1-2, Hamiltonian learning sec. 7.3.3, quantum tomography sec. 5.3.7).
figures.confirmed_by: Its content with references to relevant sections is illustrated in Fig. 1.3.

figures.confirmed_by: The dependencies between chapters are visualized as a tree in Fig. 1.4.

figures.shows: three panels. (a) binary cross-entropy L_BCE (y, 0 to about 6) against prediction f(x_i) (x, 0.0 to 1.0): for label y_i = 1 (purple, dots) the loss falls from about 5 at 0 to about 0.1 near about 0.9; for label y_i = 0 (blue) it rises from 0 to above about 6 at 1.0; the two curves cross at about 0.7 near f of 0.5. (b) regression: observed values (blue dots, y about 2 to about 6.5 over x 1 to 8), a regression line and predicted values (open circles on the line) joined to the observed values by dashed residual lines. (c) loss (y, 0 to about 5) against prediction f(x_i) (x, -2 to 2) for ground-truth label 0: MSE (purple, parabola) reaches about 4 at both ends and MAE (blue, V shape) about 2; the curves cross at about 1 near prediction of -1 and 1.
figures.confirmed_by: In the former, we also introduce the mean absolute error (MAE) as another viable loss function, which is more sensitive to small errors than the MSE as shown in Fig. 2.1(b)-(c).

figures.shows: three schematic panels of a loss curve L(theta) (y) against theta (x), no numeric scale, with a starting point (orange) and arrows for the updates: (a) too low, many tiny steps along the curve toward the minimum; (b) just right, a few larger steps that reach the minimum; (c) too high, long arrows that jump across the minimum and away from it (overshoot).
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2.2 presents in a simplified way the importance of the η choice. Both too large and too small η make optimization more challenging, and only an optimal η promises efficient convergence to a minimum.

figures.shows: three panels of two classes (green crosses and orange circles) in the x1 to x2 plane with a fitted boundary (no numbers): (a) underfitting, a straight line with points of both classes on the wrong side; (b) appropriate fitting, a smooth curve that encloses the circles with few errors; (c) overfitting, a wiggly boundary that winds around individual points.
figures.confirmed_by: The intuition behind the under- and overfitting is schematically shown in Fig. 2.3.

figures.shows: prediction error (y) against model complexity (x, low to high), no numeric scale. Both curves start at a similar high error at low complexity. The training-data curve falls steadily and flattens at a low error; the test-data curve falls to a minimum at intermediate complexity and then rises again. Arrows above mark the left side as high bias and low variance and the right side as low bias and high variance.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2.4 shows an illustration of the bias-variance trade-off, which makes clear that the ideal model realizes an optimal trade-off between the training error and the model complexity.

figures.shows: geometry of an SVM in a 2D problem. Panel (a): a two-class point set (triangles and dots) with a separating line (hyperplane), its unit vector theta* = theta/|theta|, and the projection of (x - x0) on theta* giving the distance (1/|theta|)(theta*^T x + theta0). figures.confirmed_by: For a visualization of the geometry of the data, take a look at the linearly separable problem presented in Fig. 2.5. In panel (a), you see that to classify two types of data, we can draw a line (or, more generally, a hyperplane) that separates the training data.

figures.shows: panel (a): a fully connected two-layer NN with an input layer of 6 nodes, a hidden layer of 4 nodes and an output layer of 3 nodes, labelled a(1)(x) = sigma(W(1)x + b(1)) and a(2)(x) = sigma(W(2)a(1)(x) + b(2)); panel (b): a single neuron (perceptron) with inputs x0, x1, x2 weighted by w0, w1, w2 entering a cell body that sums w_i x_i + b and applies an activation function, with biological labels (axon, dendrite, synapse, output axon). figures.shows: a convolution in two dimensions: a grid of 7 by 7 coloured circles (input), a 3 by 3 kernel of coloured circles, and a 3 by 3 output grid; a red and a green 3 by 3 window on the input are mapped to the highlighted output circles. figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2.7 illustrates the working principle behind a CNN – the convolutions: A filter (also called kernel) with trainable weights is slid across a given layer.

figures.shows: an autoencoder: an input layer of six nodes x1 to x6, a hidden bottleneck layer of three nodes a1 to a3, and an output layer of six nodes x-hat 1 to x-hat 6, fully connected between adjacent layers. No numbers beyond labels.
figures.confirmed_by: By means of a so-called bottleneck structure (as shown in Fig. 2.8), the latent representation of the input data is then mapped back into the input space (decoding) by leveraging on the information extracted by the architecture at the time of feature extraction (encoding).

figures.shows: four panels for the Ising gauge theory: upper panels show spin configurations on a square lattice at T = 0 (left, product of spins on every plaquette +1) and T to infinity (right, product +-1), one plaquette p marked in red; lower panels show the dual loop representation, closed loops on the left and loops broken at starred plaquettes on the right. No numerical axes.
figures.confirmed_by: The ground-state phase is then characterized by the property that all these loops are closed; the violation of a constraint results in the appearance of an open loop, see Fig. 3.2.

figures.shows: panel (a): a convolutional NN with filters, a fully connected layer with dropout regularization and a two-node softmax output applied to an Ising configuration; panel (b): output-layer average activation (y, 0.0 to 1.0) against T/J (x, 1.0 to 3.5) for lattice sizes L = 10, 20, 30, 40 and 60, two sigmoid-like curves (blue falling, red rising) that cross at about 2.3 where an orange vertical line (the Onsager value) lies, with a sharper crossover for larger L.
figures.confirmed_by: Remarkably, Fig. 3.4(b) shows that these activations cross over precisely at Tc enabling us to extract the correct critical temperature.

figures.shows: panel (a): the Interpretation Net, a sample configuration passing through convolutional localization networks of decreasing kernel size, an averaging layer that collapses features to a single number and a prediction network; panel (b): a Siamese NN with two identical subnetworks (Input 1 and Input 2) sharing parameters, each ending in a bottleneck (latent representation), a Compare Network and a Loss against a label. figures.confirmed_by: Therefore, the idea of the Interpretation Net is to systematically reduce the size of the kernel (and thus the input dimension for the symbolic regression task) by cutting connections until there is a significant drop in the CNN performance.

figures.shows: four example kernel functions with their mathematical forms and free parameters theta, theta1, theta2: Linear K = x^T x' + theta; Radial basis K = exp(-(1/(2 theta^2)) ||x - x'||^2); Matern 5/2 K = (1 + (sqrt 5/theta)||x - x'|| + (5/3)||x - x'||^2) exp(-(sqrt 5/theta^2)||x - x'||) as printed; Rational quadratic K = (1 + ||x - x'|| / (2 theta1 theta2^2)) to the power -theta1.

papers.what_it_is: A pedagogical review book on machine learning methods and their applications in quantum sciences, including a chapter on quantum machine learning.

existing.note: Both parts are stated on p.232 of Section 8.2.8. The book places the barren plateau in global cost functions of circuits parametrized with local unitaries, and names partial remedies (parameters close to the solution, a local cost function, correlations between parameters) that do not work well for strongly correlated systems; those points are entered as new assertions. The second part is attributed to Ref. [671].
existing.value: The authors state that a general solution to the barren-plateau problem remains an open theoretical problem, and that it is totally unclear whether there are any natural problems where a PQC will outperform a classical learning engine.
quotes: A general solution to the barren-plateau remains still an open theoretical problem.
Moreover, it is totally unclear that there are any natural problems where a PQC will outperform a classical learning engine [671].

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in a review chapter.

assertions.value: The authors define principal component analysis as identifying mutually orthogonal directions, the principal components, in the data space along which the linear correlation in the data vanishes, ranked by the variance of the data along each direction.
quotes: PCA identifies mutually orthogonal directions, called principal components (PCs), in the data space along which the linear correlation in the data vanishes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.2.1, p.54.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to reduce the dimensionality, PCA discards the principal components along which the data shows the least variance, so that directions of large variance are considered to contain the most important information.
quotes: To reduce the dimensionality of our space, we discard the PCs along which the data shows the least variance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.2.1, p.54.

assertions.value: The authors state that PCA can be understood both as variance maximization and as a minimization of a reconstruction error of a linear transformation, and refer to chapter A for the proof of this equivalence.
quotes: PCA can not only be understood as variance maximization but also as a minimization of a reconstruction error of a linear
The proof of this equivalence can be found in chapter A.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof is in the appendix chapter, not in this section.

assertions.value: The authors report that PCA applied to Ising spin configuration samples separates the data into three clusters: a high-temperature cluster for the disordered phase and two low-temperature clusters for the ordered phase with positive or negative magnetization.
quotes: For the Ising model, PCA separates the data into three clusters
as well as two low-temperature clusters corresponding to the ordered phase with either positive or negative magnetization.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.

assertions.value: The authors state that further analysis shows that the first principal component of the Ising samples corresponds to the magnetization.
quotes: shows that the first PC corresponds to the magnetization [114].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that a vertical decision boundary perpendicular to the first principal component gives a rough estimate of the critical temperature of about 2.3, which they state is in agreement with the Onsager solution.
quotes: a rough estimate of the critical transition temperature can be obtained as Tc,PCA ≈ 2.3 which is in agreement with the Onsager solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.

assertions.value: The authors report that PCA fails to cluster the Ising gauge theory data into the two prevalent phases, and attribute this to PCA being restricted to linear transformations of the input data.
quotes: In the case of the IGT, PCA fails to cluster the data into the two prevalent phases [see Fig. 3.3(c)]. This is because PCA is restricted to linear transformations of the input data.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that linear transformations are sufficient to encode simple local order parameters, such as the magnetization of the Ising model, but not to compute topological features, that is, non-local correlations in the data.
quotes: While this is sufficient to encode simple local order parameters [114–116], such as the magnetization in the case of the Ising model, linear transformations are not sufficient to compute topological features, i.e., non-local correlations in the data [116].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the limitation of PCA to linear transformations is tackled by nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, naming kernel PCA, t-SNE and UMAP.
quotes: This problem is tackled by nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, such as the kernel PCA (kPCA) [117] (see chapter 4 on the kernel trick), the t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) [118], or uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) [119].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding is a technique for nonlinear dimensionality reduction that aims to preserve the local structure of the original data, so that points close in the high-dimensional data set tend to be close in the low-dimensional representation.
quotes: are techniques for nonlinear dimensionality reduction, which aim to preserve the local structure of the original data.
That is, points that are close in the highdimensional data set tend to be close to one another in the low-dimensional representation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.2.2, p.56.

assertions.value: The authors state that in practice the perplexity used in t-SNE is usually set between 5 and 50.
quotes: In practice, the perplexity is usually set between 5 and 50.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in a review chapter.

assertions.value: The authors state that the objective of t-SNE is to find a set of points in a lower-dimensional representation, with a corresponding probability distribution, for which the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the high-dimensional distribution is minimal.
quotes: The objective of the t-SNE algorithm is to find another set of points in lower dimensional representation yi ∈ Rn×dred, dred < m and corresponding probability distribution qi j in a new representation for which the KL divergence
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.2.2, p.57.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in a review chapter.

assertions.value: The authors state that clustering combined with dimensionality reduction works elegantly for simple problems such as the Ising model, but typically does not perform well on more difficult phase classification tasks such as topological phases like the Ising gauge theory, or when a large number of phases is present.
quotes: In general, clustering in combination with dimensionality reduction works elegantly for simple problems, such as the Ising model.
However, such approaches typically do not perform well when applied to more difficult phase classification tasks
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors describe supervised phase classification as training a neural network to take spin configuration samples as input and label them by the phase they belong to, with a two-node softmax output layer and a binary cross-entropy loss; the training set holds samples far above and below the critical temperature and the test set covers the entire temperature range.
quotes: We train an NN to take spin configuration samples as input and correctly label them by the phase they belong to, see Fig. 3.4(a).

In our example, the training set consists of labeled spin configuration samples for a wide range of temperatures far above and below Tc, whereas the test set is chosen over the entire temperature range.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.3, p.58.

assertions.value: The authors report, for a neural network trained to label Ising samples by phase, that the average activations of the two output nodes cross over precisely at the critical temperature, which lets them extract the correct critical temperature.
quotes: Remarkably, Fig. 3.4(b) shows that these activations cross over precisely at Tc enabling us to extract the correct critical temperature.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: Figure 3.4 is adapted from Ref. [123].

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that the supervised neural network method is also capable of correctly identifying the crossover temperature in the Ising gauge theory.

assertions.reader_inference: This sits against the statement in Section 3.4.3 that learning by confusion has difficulty with the Ising gauge theory; the two statements concern different methods.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that a neural network trained on the square-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model can also highlight the critical temperature of the Ising model on a different lattice geometry, such as a triangular lattice.
quotes: An NN trained on configurations for the square-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model can also highlight the critical temperature of the Ising model with a different lattice geometry, such as a triangular lattice [123].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that supervised phase classification requires partial knowledge of the phase diagram of the system, namely the labels of samples deep within two neighboring phases.
quotes: Due to its supervised nature this approach requires partial knowledge of the phase diagram of the system.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.4, p.59.

assertions.value: The authors report that the latent representation of an autoencoder trained to reconstruct Ising Monte Carlo samples clusters into two groups that correspond to the two phases of the Ising model.

assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that clustering of data in the latent space according to the phases of the system is not a general property of autoencoders; it occurs when the input data cause distinctive activations in the bottleneck, which often corresponds to different phases.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in a review chapter.

assertions.value: The authors describe a scheme in which an autoencoder is trained to reconstruct states from one phase and then used on the rest of the phase diagram, so that the reconstruction error is expected to vary with the phases and phase boundaries, which enables phase discovery in a fully unsupervised way.
quotes: Imagine training an AE to reconstruct states coming from one phase. Then, the AE is used to reconstruct states coming from the rest of the phase diagram.
This scheme enables the discovery of phases in a fully unsupervised way.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the authors of Ref. [126] used the anomaly detection scheme to recover a full phase diagram of the extended Bose-Hubbard model in one dimension at exact integer filling.

assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cited work also revealed, within the phase diagram, a phase-separated region with unexpected properties, which may be one of the first fully unsupervised discoveries in ML-guided phase classification.

assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors describe learning by confusion as partitioning the temperature range into two regions with distinct labels, training a supervised classifier over the entire range, recording the classification accuracy for that guess of the critical temperature, repeating for many bi-partitions, and plotting accuracy against the guessed critical temperature, where each partitioning requires the training of a separate neural network.
quotes: We start by partitioning the temperature range into two regions with distinct labels.
Note that each partitioning requires the training of a separate NN.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classification accuracy of learning by confusion applied to the Ising model is W-shaped, with high accuracy at the extremes of the temperature range because almost all samples are then assigned the same label, and a non-trivial middle peak that corresponds to the predicted critical temperature.
quotes: We observe that the classification accuracy is W-shaped.
The middle peak, however, is non-trivial and corresponds to the predicted critical temperature of the method.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.

assertions.value: The authors state that when all samples are assigned the same label a classification accuracy of one can be achieved trivially, because the network only needs to output the same label independent of the input.
quotes: In particular, in the extreme case where all samples are assigned the same label a classification accuracy of 1 can be achieved trivially because the NN simply needs to learn to output the same label independent of the input.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 3.4.2, p.61.

quotes: We fix the parameters of the Hamiltonian to J = [1, 1, −1] and h = [1, 1.5, 3].
These parameters are chosen to be far away from any phase transition point, not to make the problem too difficult.
The ansatz consists in two rotation gates, applied to every qubits in Y and Z direction, three CNOT gates that connect every qubits, and two more rotations in Y and Z direction.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states or derives this in Section 8.2.6, p.230.

assertions.value: The authors state that on a classical computer the cost of evaluating the energy would scale exponentially with the number of qubits, while on a perfect quantum computer the expectation value of the Hamiltonian can be computed efficiently with a cost linear in the number of qubits.
quotes: the computational cost of the evaluation of the energy would scale exponentially with the number of qubits.
The expectation value of the Hamiltonian of the system can be computed efficiently on a perfect quantum computer. The computational cost is linear in the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in a review chapter.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement assumes a perfect quantum computer, which the NISQ section of the book says does not yet exist.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the Nelder-Mead optimizer, the four-spin Heisenberg VQE finds a relatively good approximation of the ground-state energy with few variational parameters and polynomial computational cost in the number of qubits.
quotes: in this case, we use the Nelder-Mead optimization routine.
We can find a relatively good approximation of the ground-state energy with few variational parameters and polynomial computational cost in the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: A single illustrative simulation; no error value is given in the text.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 8.16: the energy of the four-spin Heisenberg VQE falls from about -2 at the first optimization step to about -16 within about 300 steps, and then stays on the exact-solution line, whose value is about -16.
quotes: Figure 8.16: An example of a variational quantum simulation.
In Fig. 8.16(b), we plot the value of the energy of the system as a function of the optimization step.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement or derivation in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: Read by eye; the energy axis has no unit label.

assertions.value: The authors state that VQE simulations can be improved in the ansatz design, for example by imposing symmetries, and in the optimization routine, with gradient-based or gradient-free methods such as Bayesian optimization, and that a cited work derives a kernel inspired by the parameter shift rule to update VQE parameters accurately with fewer measurements.
quotes: In the design of variational quantum circuits, we can, for example, impose symmetries of the system we are studying.
the authors derive a novel kernel, inspired by the parameter shift rule to update the VQE parameters accurately with less measurements on the quantum computer.

assertions.value: The authors state that for classification with variational quantum circuits the first non-trivial task is loading the classical data on the quantum hardware, and that Ref. [668] showed a PQC with data reuploading can lead to a good classifier.

classification on symmetry-protected topological phase in the Haldane chain directly from the quantum state, that can be obtained with a VQE.

assertions.value: The authors state that possible solutions to the barren-plateau problem are using parameters close to the solution, using a local cost function instead of a global one, or introducing correlations between parameters, but that these methods do not work well for strongly correlated systems.

papers.what_it_is: A short proposal of a hybrid quantum kernel classifier with a two-qubit inner-product circuit, tested in a noiseless simulator on a synthetic inside-or-outside-a-circle task.

existing.note: The paper limits the result: it comes from one noiseless statevector simulation, and the 99% is measured on 100 new random points in the square; the authors say the larger learned radius is only suggested. The page numbers in the stored anchor are journal pages; the PDF pages are p.9 (Portuguese results) and p.11 (English abstract).
existing.value: The authors report that, in a noiseless statevector simulation, a shift value computed from the training grid classified 99% of 100 new random points in the square correctly, 100% of the points inside the circle and 98% of those outside, and state that this suggests the circle learned by the kernel method has a slightly larger radius than the one used to generate the training outputs.
quotes: valor de deslocamento para 100 novos pontos aleatórios no interior do
100% dos pontos no interior e 98% dos pontos no exterior
Este simulador não inclui ruídos, ele é um simulador de
It was found that the algorithm was able to correctly detect new points in 99% of the samples tested, with a small difference due to considering the radius slightly larger than the ideal.
existing.reader_inference: The test set is 100 points from one random draw; 98% of the points outside is one or two points of the roughly half of 100 that fall outside the circle, so the numbers carry large sampling error.

figures.shows: An overview of the compilation chain: an 'Open Graph' (a honeycomb lattice of hexagons) is decomposed into a 'Fusion Network' (the same lattice with some edges marked as X or Y fusions), then a 'Fusion Pattern' (a command sequence of corrections, measurements, fusions, entangling gates and preparations) and an 'Optical Protocol' (a circuit diagram with an emitter, a delay module D_sigma, a fusion module F, a correction module C and a measurement module M). Arrows run from graph to network, to pattern and to protocol. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: as a translation between four concepts: graphs, networks, patterns and protocols.

figures.shows: Panel (a): linear-optical resource graphs (a star, a ring, a complete-like graph). Panel (b): matter-based resource graphs (a single emitter, a linear cluster, a branching linear structure). Panel (c): the action of a Type-II fusion measurement on two graph states: on success (s) the two graph states are merged through a new node; on failure (F) each keeps its structure with the fused nodes disconnected or changed. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: Examples of photonic graph states used in the literature include the star graph [34, 39], rings [5] and completelike graphs [55].

papers.what_it_is: A formal (category-theoretic and ZX-calculus) framework for photonic fusion-based quantum computing, with theorems on correctable fusion measurements, a flow structure for fusion networks, repeat-until-success fusion protocols, and universality of a single-emitter architecture in an idealized setting.
